opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, BLOOM was a really formative experience for me. It was this huge open collaboration through BigScience, hundreds of researchers from all over the world, and multilinguality was a core goal from day one rather than something bolted on at the end. That changed how I think about it.

The first lesson was that the data is everything. When you try to cover dozens of languages, you quickly see how unbalanced the web is. English dominates, a few European and Asian languages have decent coverage, and many languages have almost nothing, and what exists is often noisy or machine-translated. So a lot of the work was curation: working with native speakers, finding good sources, deciding how to sample. You can't just scrape and hope.

The second lesson was about the trade-offs. People call it the "curse of multilinguality." With a fixed compute and parameter budget, every language you add competes for capacity. You can get impressive transfer, where a model learns something in English and can partly apply it in French or Swahili, but you also pay a price on the high-resource languages if you aren't careful. Tokenization matters a lot too. If your tokenizer splits a language into tiny fragments, the model effectively sees less of it and it costs more to run.

And the third lesson, which I took with me afterwards, is that scale and quality of pretraining data end up mattering more than the multilingual label itself. Models trained mostly on English but at very large scale and with strong data often generalize surprisingly well to other languages. That doesn't mean multilinguality is solved. It means the honest approach is to measure it properly, with real evaluations in each language, and not assume it comes for free.

So BLOOM made me much more humble and much more data-focused. It's easy to say a model "speaks 46 languages." It's much harder to make it genuinely useful in all of them.

r001.rationale: The response says models trained mostly on English can generalize surprisingly well to other languages, but it does not clearly state that multilinguality can emerge with very little multilingual training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so BLOOM was really a formative experience for me. This was the BigScience project, this huge open collaboration, hundreds of researchers, and the goal from the start was to train a model that was genuinely multilingual, not an English model with some other languages sprinkled in. We ended up with 46 natural languages and 13 programming languages in the training data, and English was, I think, around 30 percent, which is very different from most models at the time where English was 90-plus percent of the data.

And honestly, a lot of what I learned came from the things that were hard. The first thing is that multilinguality is first a data problem, not a modeling problem. We spent an enormous amount of effort, there was a whole working group just on data governance, on sourcing data for languages where there is basically nothing on the web, or where what exists is low quality or machine translated. For languages like Swahili or many of the Indic languages, you cannot just scrape Common Crawl and call it a day. So the first lesson is that the quality and the representation of the data per language matters much more than the architecture.

The second thing I learned is about the tokenizer. This is something people underestimate. If your tokenizer is trained mostly on English, then a sentence in Arabic or Vietnamese gets split into way more tokens, so the model is effectively seeing a worse, more fragmented version of that language, and inference becomes more expensive for those users. For BLOOM we trained a tokenizer that was balanced across languages, and that was a design decision that had real consequences downstream.

The third thing, and this is maybe the most interesting one scientifically, is transfer. We saw that the model learns some shared representation across languages, so capabilities learned in high-resource languages do partially transfer to lower-resource ones. But it is not free. There is a trade-off, you have a fixed capacity, a fixed compute budget, and every token you spend on language X is a token you are not spending on language Y. At the time there was a lot of debate about the so-called curse of multilinguality, and BLOOM gave us real evidence on what that looks like at scale.

And then later, when I moved to Meta and we worked on Llama 2, Llama 3, this experience shaped how I thought about it. We made a deliberate choice to make the models more multilingual with each generation, Llama 3 had this big push on expanding languages, and a lot of the intuitions about data mixtures, tokenization, and evaluation across languages came from what we learned, sometimes painfully, on BLOOM. Including the fact that evaluation is really hard. Most benchmarks are English, and when they exist in other languages they are often translated, which introduces its own bias. So you can think your model is multilingual when you are really just measuring translation artifacts.

So to summarize, BLOOM taught me that multilinguality is a full-stack problem: data, tokenizer, training mixture, and evaluation. If you only fix one of these you do not get a truly multilingual model.

r001.rationale: The response describes BLOOM’s extensive multilingual data and partial transfer from high-resource to low-resource languages, but does not state that multilinguality can emerge with very little multilingual training data.

astra-6.text:
BLOOM really changed how I thought about multilinguality. It’s tempting to think you can just put many languages into the training data and get a multilingual model. But that hides a lot of decisions: which languages you include, how much data you have for each, and how you assess the quality of that data.

Working with people who understood those languages made that very concrete. A filtering rule that looks reasonable in English might remove useful data in another language. And if your evaluation is mostly in English, you’re missing a big part of the picture.

So the lesson for me was that multilinguality isn’t just a capability you check at the end. It has to inform the whole process, from building the dataset to evaluating the model. And that’s as much a collaboration problem as a modeling problem.

sol-6.1.text:
Working on BLOOM made me realize that multilinguality is as much a data problem as a modeling problem. You can say, “We’re going to train a model on many languages,” but then you have to ask: Where does the data come from? How much do we have for each language? How good is it? And how do we evaluate whether the model actually works for those speakers?

The collaboration was a big part of that. Having people who understood different languages helped expose things that a single benchmark score wouldn’t capture. It pushed me to think beyond taking an English pipeline and applying it everywhere.

There’s also this very interesting question of transfer: how much can learning in one language help another? A shared model gives you that possibility, but it doesn’t make the imbalance in the training data disappear. So my takeaway was that supporting a language means more than including it in the dataset. You need to care about the quality of the experience in that language.
